backTranslations.41:
**Before the visit**
- In the Visits tab, add the appointment date. MenoMap shows how prepared your notes are and what would make them more complete.
- Pick the most important topics and questions, three or four is enough.
- Make notes for the past 30 or 90 days, and confirm your medication list is up to date.

**During the visit**
- Hand the first page to the doctor or show it to them. This page is designed to be read within a minute: counts, averages, heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question you care about most.
- If your doctor uses another language, you can make the notes in that language.

**What the notes are and are not**

The notes are a summary of what you entered, plus data you chose to import from the Health app. The notes are not a diagnosis and not a complete medical record; any patterns in them are only coincidence checks and cannot prove cause and effect. The doctor may ask questions the notes cannot answer, which is normal.

**After the visit**

Add any new medication and its start date. After a few weeks, MenoMap can show your records before and after you started the medication, making the assessment at the next follow-up easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a point in time: the day after 12 consecutive months without a period, and which cannot be explained by other causes (such as pregnancy, certain medications, or surgery). In many countries it happens on average in the early 50s, but between around 45 and around 55 is common.

**The menopause transition** is the years before reaching that point. Hormone levels fluctuate, so periods can become irregular, heavier or lighter, with shorter or longer gaps. Many changes people associate with the change of life, such as hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and mood changes, often begin at this stage, while periods still come. The transition can last a few years or longer, and it differs for everyone.

**Postmenopause** is all the time after the full 12 months. Some symptoms ease over time, some may continue for many years.

Menopause can also happen early because of surgery removing the ovaries, certain cancer treatments or other health conditions. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and is worth discussing with a doctor.

**How it is determined.** For many people over 45, the doctor judges from your history and symptoms whether you are in the transition or have reached menopause. Blood tests are not necessarily needed, because hormone levels vary daily. Blood tests are more likely to be arranged when younger or when the situation is unclear.

**What MenoMap can and cannot do.** MenoMap cannot tell you which stage you are in. What it can do is faithfully record what you notice: hot flashes, sleep, mood and treatments, so you and your doctor see the same overall picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden rush of heat, often appearing on the face, neck and chest, sometimes with skin flushing, sweating, rapid heartbeat, or feeling cold afterwards. Night sweats are the same thing happening during sleep, and can be so intense they wake you with heat or soak the sheets.

They are among the most common changes around the change of life. Some people have only a few mild episodes; some have several a day, affecting work and sleep. Some people find them fade within a few years, some find they last longer.

**What may make them more likely.** People often find they are related to alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, stuffy hot rooms, stress or heavy bedding. These factors vary greatly from person to person, so tracking your own labels may be more useful than a generic list.

**There are other causes too.** Skin flushing and sweating can also come from thyroid problems, infection, certain medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not fit the usual pattern, or come with weight loss, fever or feeling unwell, tell the doctor.

**Describing them well.** Useful details at a visit:
- Roughly how many times in the day and at night
- How intense they feel and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversation, exercise
- What seemed to happen before an episode
- What you have tried, and whether it made any change

MenoMap's hot flash button and after-the-fact logging feature are meant to record this information effortlessly.

**There are ways to help.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, and some practical methods. Which suit you needs to be discussed with the doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT or MHT) replaces part of the estrogen the body produces less of around the change of life. Major medical guidelines consider that for many people it is an effective way to treat hot flashes and night sweats, and may also help improve other symptoms.

**There are different forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets, and low-dose vaginal products used to improve local symptoms (such as dryness). People who still have a uterus usually use progestogen together with the estrogen, to protect the uterine lining.

**Benefits and risks vary by person:** depending on age, how long since menopause, personal and family medical history (such as breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease), and the type of treatment and route of use. So this is a decision to make with a doctor who knows your history, not one an app can make for you.

**Common questions:**
- Is hormone therapy right for me? Why or why not?
- Which type and form would you recommend? Why?
- What benefits can I expect? How soon will it work?
- What are my personal risks? How do they compare with not treating?
- What should I watch for? When should it be re-evaluated?

**If you are already using it,** record it in MenoMap (Me → Medications). MenoMap shows your hot flashes before and after you started, which is only a coincidence check, not evidence, giving you something concrete to discuss at a follow-up assessment.

MenoMap never recommends starting, stopping or changing any medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not right for everyone, and some people simply prefer to take another route. There are several other options.

**Prescription options.** Some non-hormonal medications have evidence of reducing hot flashes. These include certain medications originally developed for other conditions, and a new class of medication designed specifically for hot flashes. Each medication has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, and a doctor can help you weigh them.

**Talking and mind-body therapies.** Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) adapted for the change of life has evidence that it makes hot flashes and night sweats less troublesome and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis also has related research.

**Practical changes many people find helpful:**
- Wear layers that can be removed quickly
- Put a fan on the desk and by the bed
- Keep the bedroom a bit cool, use breathable bedding
- Notice and reduce personal triggers (MenoMap's labels and experiments can help)
- Be active regularly, keep a steady sleep routine

**Nutritional supplements and herbal products.** For many of these products the evidence is mixed or limited, quality varies, and some interact with other medications. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about any product you use, including non-prescription products.

**Try only one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiment compares your own records before the change and during the change, making it easier to judge than going by feeling alone.

backTranslations.416:
Most appointments are short, and it is not easy to recall a whole month of nights on the spot. People often remember only the last few days, or the hardest ones. A simple record can fill that gap.

**What a diary can give the doctor:**
- How often symptoms occur and how intense, not just whether they occur
- Whether things are improving, getting worse, or staying the same
- What was happening around them: sleep, drinking, stress, medication
- A starting point for comparison if you try a treatment

**Keep logging easy.** A diary is only helpful if kept up. MenoMap is built around a tap-to-log hot flash button and a four-question evening review, which takes just seconds, no need to fill a notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Two to four weeks of records usually show a clearer picture than a single bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptoms that trouble you most, what you want to try or avoid, and anything that worries you. MenoMap's Visits tab can help you pick questions and print them together with the notes.

backTranslations.479:
Once there have been 12 consecutive months without a period, **any vaginal bleeding should be checked by a doctor**, even if it has happened only once, even if it is only spotting, or only a light pink or brown discharge.

In most cases the cause turns out not to be serious, for example thinning of the vaginal lining or uterine lining is very common. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition, and such conditions are much easier to treat when found early. This is why public health guidance recommends getting checked rather than waiting.

**If you are using hormone therapy,** depending on the type you use, some bleeding patterns may be expected. Bleeding that is not expected for your therapy, heavier than usual, or at a time when it should not occur, should also be checked.

**What to do:**
- Contact your doctor or health facility, and say you have had bleeding after menopause.
- Note the date, the amount of bleeding, and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can help you keep this information (Me → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you the cause of the bleeding. It will remind you to get checked, and put the bleeding record in your visit notes.

backTranslations.529:
Sleeping badly is one of the most common troubles in midlife, and it rarely has just a single cause.

**Night sweats** may wake you directly, or make you too hot or wet to fall asleep again.

**Other common contributing factors:**
- Needing to get up to urinate at night
- Anxiety or a mind that will not stop
- Alcohol, which may help you fall asleep but often makes the second half of the night's sleep fragmented
- Caffeine later in the day
- Pain, restless legs syndrome, or a partner's snoring
- Snoring or pauses in breathing during sleep, which may be a sign of sleep apnea (worth raising, especially if very sleepy in the daytime)

**What usually helps people.** A cool, dim room; breathable bedding and removable layers; a fixed wake-up time; and less alcohol before bed. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-studied method, and many doctors can refer you.

**What to track.** For a week or two, note your sleep score, night hot flashes, drinking and late caffeine. MenoMap's evening review and hot flash log take just a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app alongside night sweats, as background information, not an explanation.

**When to get checked.** If poor sleep affects your safety (such as driving), mood or daily life, or you notice pauses in breathing or gasping at night, talk to a doctor.
